title: Using Curiosity & Wonder to Guide Inquiry
before:
Students are naturally curious about the world around them. In this module, explore how to activate and use your students' curiosity and wonder to guide inquiry-based instruction.

Introduction
Starter Kit

Here are five strategies for designing inquiries around your students' questions and wonderings. To learn more, check out the additional resources below.

decisions.label: Tag a document link with the format it opens
decisions.why: 1 link on this page opens a file — 1 Video — and says nothing about it, while others in the same list carry a tag because their author typed one. The format is read from the file name, so the list stops being half-labelled. No link text changes.

decisions.label: Drop the dash once the link is set apart
decisions.why: 2 of those items separate the link from its description with a dash. The link is now set in the display face at a larger size with a chevron after it, so the dash marks a boundary that is already unmistakable. Only the separator is removed — no word changes.

decisions.label: Separate a link from its description
decisions.why: 2 list items open with a link and then explain it, all at the same weight — so the thing you can click is no easier to find than the sentence about it. The link becomes the item and the explanation sits under it.

decisions.label: Use this paragraph as the page description
decisions.why: It is the page’s own opening paragraph, moved into the banner rather than rewritten.
decisions.value: Students are naturally curious about the world around them. In this module, explore how to activate and use your students' curiosity and wonder to guide inquiry-based instruction.

decisions.label: Retire the old banner graphic
decisions.why: It repeats the page title in picture form, which the new banner already does in type.
decisions.removes: Interdisciplinary Instruction -using curiosity and wonder to guide inquiry banner .png

decisions.label: Let a bold line dividing a card be its heading
decisions.why: 5 lines inside the cards are a paragraph holding nothing but a few bold words — "Sites" is one — with the part of the card it names underneath. That is a heading, and set as a paragraph it carries no level, so the card offers nothing to scan by and a screen reader announces only running text. Each becomes an h3 and takes the same section bar the other card headings use. Only where a card has two or more, which is what makes them divisions rather than one stressed line. Not a word changes.
